reasoning.rule: A §138 offence requires a legally enforceable debt, and the dishonour reason must fall within the statute's own words or settled case law
reasoning.plainEnglish: The debt is confirmed as legally enforceable, and the bank's reason (insufficient funds) is squarely within §138's own text. Proceed.

reasoning.rule: The cheque must be presented within its period of validity
reasoning.source: NI Act §138 proviso (a); RBI directive effective 01 Apr 2012 (validity reduced from 6 months to 3)
reasoning.countingRule: Exclude the trigger day; add 3 calendar months, clamped to month-end
reasoning.plainEnglish: The cheque is dated 20 Jul 2026 and stays valid for presentation until 20 Oct 2026. It was presented on 22 Jul 2026, well within that window.

recoveryPath.source: MSR Leathers v. S. Palaniappan (2013) 1 SCC 177
recoveryPath.plainEnglish: The 30-day notice window closed on 24 Aug 2026 without a notice being sent, but the cheque itself is still valid for presentation until 20 Oct 2026. You can re-present it any time before then. Re-presentation creates a fresh dishonour and restarts the entire chain — fresh presentation, fresh 30-day notice window, fresh notice, fresh 15-day payment wait, fresh 1-month filing window — not just a new notice deadline on the old one.

reasoning.rule: A demand notice must be sent within 30 days of learning of the dishonour
reasoning.source: NI Act §138 proviso (b); day-counting per §9 General Clauses Act 1897, applied in Econ Antri Ltd v. Rom Industries Ltd (2014) 11 SCC 769
reasoning.countingRule: Exclude the trigger day; deadline = trigger + 30 days
reasoning.plainEnglish: You learned of the dishonour on 25 Jul 2026. The notice needed to be sent by 24 Aug 2026. Today is 17 Sep 2026 and no notice has been sent — this window is closed. Condonation does not apply here; that only covers a late complaint (Clock 4), not a late notice.
